(Canadian press). Toronto, Ont. March 12.
With sales totalling $55,360,569, the liquor control commission reported a profit for 1929 of $9,661,448-
A profit.
-it was revealed in the annual statement of the year tabled in the legislature to-day by the government.
That is a profit of nearly $10,000,000 in the province of Ontario alone in a single year out of the liquor traffic. An amount exceeding the total grants to the provinces for technical education by the federal government during the past ten years. I think the province of Ontario, if I may be permitted to advise the provincial government that far, could not do a better thing than earmark all that money for technical education.
May I ask the Prime Minister a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How much money did the federal treasury collect in excise tax on liquor during the same period?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend will get full particulars of that to-morrow or a little later. When my hon. friend asks us to appropriate $1,000,000 a year by way of federail grants to the provinces in aid of technical education, I think it is only fair to remind him that we have obligations to meet to-day such as we never had before, and to draw his attention to the fact that one of the provinces which would get the largest portion of this grant has this year a surplus of nearly $10,000,000 solely from the operation of its liquor stores. That condition is very different from the one the province of Ontario faced at the time the federal government made grants to the provinces in aid of technical education. What has happened in Ontario is true also of Quebec, and true also, only in lesser degree, of practically all the other provinces. They all have government liquor control with its monopoly of sales for domestic consumption within the province.
Not all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are all making profits out of the sale of liquor. Prince Edward Island is not.
Nor Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, in view of the decision of the province, I venture to say it will not be very long before Nova Scotia has a liquor control commission. At any rate it will have it in operation during the period that my hon. friend wants these grants in aid of technical education to be made. I think it would be an admirable thing, and I think it would meet with the approval of the citizens of each province, if the respective provincial governments would -talce, if not all, at least half of the profits from the sale of liquor and devote the money thus secured to technical education. Then they would be carrying out some of Carlyle's diet-urns and wishes and the wishes of some of the people of this country.
My hon. friend has asked me a few questions. First of all he asks, do I hold that Canada does not need technical education. Of course I hold that Canada needs technical education. Every word that I said at any time on the necessity for and benefits of technical education I am prepared to stand by at the present time, every word. I believe that Canada needs technical education, but I believe that Canada is in a much better position in the matter of technical schools to-day than she has ever hitherto been. We

Technical Education-Mr. Mackenzie King
find a great difference between the position when these grants were first made and the position to-day. Already the federal government has spent between $8,000,000 and S9.-000,000 on technical schools in the different provinces, and the provinces themselves have spent an equal amount or more, and to-day they are carrying on these technical schools without making any change whatever. I ask my hon. friend to tell me where one single teacher has been dropped, where one school has been closed, in any of the provinces since the federal grant has ceased.

Pardon me, sir. Since we have lost the federal aid to technical education the government of British Columbia has issued to the various technical schools a statement that they could not continue the grant which had previously been made by the Dominion government, and therefore they were not able to meet the requirements of the technical, domestic science, and manual schools. Consequently those schools are suffering now from the cessation of that aid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel -constrained1 to say a word in respect to the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich), because I feel that the education of the youth of Canada is -perhaps one of the most important problems with which any -public body must deal.
I am of the opinion, as I am sure many other Canadians are, that the system of general education in this country to-day is entirely wrong. It is based on one line of study, and one line only; from the moment a boy or girl enters our public schools, his or her system of education runs along one line, which leads to the university. They are taught subjects which qualify them for entrance to
university only. For what are the boys and girls fitted who have passed into the high school, have for three or four years attended high school or collegiate institute, and secured admittance to the university? I would like to ask one or two of my h-on. friends that question. Can they go into a store and keep a set of books? No; they have not been educated along those lines. Will they go out on the farm and work there? No; they have too much education for that. Will they learn a trade; will they learn carpentering, black-smithing, or any of the mechanical pursuits? Not at all; they have n-ot been educated along those lines. They have been taught a smattering of imperfect French, Latin, Greek, geometry, algebra, chemistry and physics, subjects absolutely useless to ordinary men and women in this life. We forget that ninety per cent of the boys and girls in this country never see a university; we forget that it is our duty to educate these boys and girls to be good citizens o-f Canada, and we are able to do that only through technical education. We should have a system which would pla-ce in the minds of our teachers a sufficient knowledge of psychology to enable them to detect in a boy of fourteen or fifteen years of age whethenr he would be a good mechanic, or to tell whether a boy or a girl should follow a profession and, if they show an aptitude for professional studies, whether they should go on to the university. In other words, let them be taught along the lines which will equip them for really useful citizenehi-p in this country.
My hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has told -us there is a balance of $1,614,448 still unpaid out of the grant formerly provided for in aid of technical education. We are making no comment as to that. What we in Canada want him to do, however, is to -continue the grant for the children who attend those schools, and make certain that our boys and girls will receive technical education. He spoke o-f the sum of $9,000,000 being collected in the past yea' as profit on the sale of liquor in the province of Ontario. That is true, but let me tell him that over $10,000,000 was expended by the same province last year in aid o-f education. I am not speaking for Ontario alone; I speak for the whole Dominion o-f Canada, and I feel that this government should take heed of the situation as it exists.
The Prime Minister has said that education is a provincial matter; we will admit -that. What is he doing with our money? Is he spending it broadcast throughout Canada? Why, the bulk of the money is being spent right here in the city of Ottawa in the de-
582	COMMONS
Technical Education-Mr. Cantley
struction of public property. He has spent $4,000,000 in this city; let him devote half that amount to the education of the boys and girls of Canada, and he will be doing something; he will be rendering a real service to our people.
The Prime Minister told us that the Ontario liquor control board collected $9,000,000 in profits in the past year, knowing full well that this Dominion placed in its pockets $53,000,000 by the tax on liquor. Why not give us half of that; why not give us a quarter or an eighth of that amount in aid of technical education? Then every Canadian will hold up both his hands in favour of Mackenzie King as one of the greatest advocates of technical education we have ever known.
The Prime Minister speaks of industrial research. What connection has industrial research with the education of our boys and girls? We must agree that industrial research is a wonderful thing; we believe it is necessary, and something which will pay back tenfold every dollar spent. What we are interested in, however, in connection with this particular resolution, is the education of the youth of this land, and I say to the government of this country that it is their duty to place in the estimates a grant in aid of technical education and give the boys and girls of Canada a real chance.

I did not intend to take part in this discussion, and I shall keep the house but a very few minutes. My reason for speaking is to emphasize the need for technical education at this time. The need increases as we change our methods of life, not only in the city but on the farms. The time has come when we need trained men for agriculture. With our present fiscal system there is a concentration of wealth in the great industrial centres, and the agricultural provinces are finding themselves unable to meet their obligations.
I sympathize with the Prime Minister (Mr Mackenzie King) in his endeavour to keep provincial and Dominion matters apart, because I believe they should be kept apart. But my main reason for rising to-night was to discuss a rather strange recommendation. Canada is a member of the League of Nations, which has done splendid work in either deterring or stopping the sale of drugs which dull the intellect of our people. I was sorry to hear the Prime Minister throw out the suggestion that Ontaria could use for technical education a large part of the revenue derived from the liquor business. Are our young people to come to the conclusion that it is all right to sell liquor

in order to give them education? I regret that these economic questions are not considered in relation to their moral effect upon the citizens of Canada. I am sorry to hear the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Maloney) speak as though he were jealous of the revenue derived by the Dominion from the liquor traffic.
It is not my intention to keep the house any longer. As I have said, I sympathize with the Prime Minister and believe that he is right in keeping provincial and Dominion matters apart, but I did feel that I should make some comment upon the phases of the subject to which I have referred. I believe that when the provinces took over the distribution of liquor the underlying motive was to sell as little as possible, and I was sorry to hear the recommendation thrown out that the profits derived from that business should be used for the education of our young people.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest and with some pleasure to some of the remarks made to-night, but I was particularly interested in what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said regarding this matter.
One of his favourite expressions is the implements of production, and I would like to point out that in my judgment the most important implements of production in this country are the trained intellects and hands of the workers, artisans and fanners. If Canada is to hold its own with the other nations of the world, and particularly with our neighbour to the south, we must have more of those trained implements. Private concerns in the United States are devoting as much as $1,000,000 in some cases and I believe as high as $3,000,000 yearly to industrial research in connection with their own particular industry. It must be realized that we in the Dominion of Canada with our limited resources and comparatively small industrial enterprises do labour and will continue to labour under great handicaps.
The Prime Minister contends that the matter of technical education is not one for the federal government, but I am sorry that as to that I cannot agree with him. While, as he observed, the obligations placed upon the federal government have grown enormously during the last twenty years, so have its resources. Apart from the one source of revenue to which reference has been made by him, the resources of the smaller provinces have not increased in proportion to the obligations imposed upon them. Take the one matter of improved highways. The province of Nova Scotia is spending close to one-half

Technical Education-Mr. Bennett
of its yearly revenues upon road improvement, and that proportion will in all probability increase as the years go by. The Prime Minister has referred to what is being done in scientific research and to the amount of money which will be expended this year and in succeeding years in connection with that matter. That is all to the good, but I want to say this:	So far as much of the work which has
been done in that connection in this city is concerned it has been for the most part actually wasted. So-called research has been carried on in this city for the last four or five years which is not scientific research at all. Money is being squandered in connection with reputed research work of the Mines department, which has been playing with experiments which have been worked out in practical experience in industrial concerns, in some cases almost twenty years ago. So far as I know there has not been one single important fact demonstrated or anything approaching a scientific discovery made by that department since I came to this house five years ago.
N otwithstanding the defence offered by the Prime Minister for the position he takes, I must differ from him and I still think this question is one of the most important matters brought before the house, and that a duty lies upon the federal government which cannot be put upon the provincial governments, particularly of the smaller provinces. In view of and considering the necessities confronting them, which are yearly augmented, they are unable to cope with the situation; therefore the smaller provinces require aid to a greater degree than do the larger provinces. Could we, I ask, in Nova Scotia begin to give our young people the technical education which the province of Ontario, with its larger revenues, supplies, containing as it does so many large industrial enterprises?
The Prime Minister referred to the royal commission appointed some years ago to look into this question of technical education. I well remember the personnel of that commission which took evidence in the various provinces. It sat in my home town of New Glasgow in Nova Scotia, and I had the opportunity of giving evidence before it. Its work was highly beneficial, as it aroused the interest of the whole country in the question. I contend that the federal government has not as yet undertaken its share of that work, the importance of which it surely realized when it appointed that commission. I appeal to the Prime Minister to revise his views in connection with this matter. I do not think the government can dispose of its obligations
quite as easily as the Prime Minister would lead us to suppose, or on the ground that he
suggests.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to trespass upon the time of the house in discussing this matter at any great length, but this I will say: the Dominion parliament has for years voted a sum of money to aid the provinces in technical education. That became necessary because of the inability of the provinces to expend, out of their own resources, the money that might be necessary to establish technical schools upon a proper basis. The increased burden of taxation imposed upon the provinces has been so great that in some instances on a mere quarter-section of land it amounts to twenty times what it did before the war. I am sorry to say that is so. There never before has been a time when there was greater necessity for such grants being continued to the provinces than there is to-day. That can be readily realized by anyone who will take the trouble to look into the condition of the western provinces and the burden of taxation they must bear. Anyone who lives in Manitoba will agree with that, having regard to the necessities of that province during the last few years in the increased burden of taxation imposed upon the people of that province. Anyone in Saskatchewan who realizes the necessity of the supplementary taxes that have been imposed in that province will also agree, and the same thing is true in regard to Alberta. Therefore if it was right to initiate this grant, it is right to continue it at the present time to an even greater degree than at any other time. The provinces have entered upon and expended sums of money in respect of an undertaking which they now must cany on, and which they would not have entered upon had it not been for the aid they received from the federal government. Under those circumstances, the provinces having received that aid, I earnestly hope it may be continued.
Now I go to the second point: It is said that this is a matter of grace and favour. The technical schools are the universities for the poor boys and girls of Canada. Those who cannot afford to take education in the universities must secure through these technical schools the training necessary to fit them for the trades and occupations in which they engage, even domestic science. The school, for instance, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchko-vich), is one that has been doing great service in the city of Calgary and in the southern part of Alberta.
SS4	COMMONS
Technical Education-Mr. Bennett
As I have passed through Canada during the last two years and have seen the technical schools that have been erected under the provisions of the grant that has been made for technical education, I realize that a valuable service has been rendered to this country through the money devoted to that purpose. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) contends that the greatest obligation that can rest upon a government of this country is to extend our trade. How can we compete in foreign countries and extend our markets unless we have men and women in factories, machine shops and industries -who by their training are enabled to produce goods and commodities with as much skill as their competitors in those markets, and to use with equal effectiveness and efficiency the machines employed in that production? And how are we to do that except through technical training? It is a matter of trade and commerce; it is a matter of Dominion, not merely of provincial concern, and because it is a matter of trade and commerce, because it is a matter of the extension of our export business throughout the world, because it is a matter of enabling the youth of the country, who may not go to the universities, to be so equipped that they may be able with skill of hand and eye to utilize to the fullest effect the machines employed in industry and in the various productive enterprises upon which our export business depends, I submit that the federal government should make that contribution to technical education. In that sense it does not conflict with research, industrial or scientific. Industrial and scientific investigations are carried on by specialists, skilled scientific minds, trained products of universities, men and women who have had academic training, but the technical schools are not for that purpose. They are for one purpose only, namely, to enable the trade and commerce of this country to be extended in competition with the trade and commerce of other countries where men and women are thus trained.
In the United States the very measure to which the hon. member referred enables the federal treasury to make grants in order that cooperation between the federal and state authorities will equip the men and women trained in their technical schools to send their products to every part of the world in as good condition, produced as cheaply and as efficiently, as those which come from Germany and other countries. In a message to the people of England, the late Lord Haldane, speaking of technical education, said that what gave Germany her preeminence in world [Mr. BeanettJ
trade before the great war was the fact that her boys and girls had received technical education under a scheme that had been unheard of in Europe prior to that time. He said: "Until this kingdom realizes what its duties are with respect to technical education, we shall never be able to overtake our competitors in the industrial race." So that following the war one of the important matters to which Great Britain, France and Germany are directing attention is technical education, and we Canadians must compete with them in the markets of the world. We must go to China, to Japan, to the orient, to every market of the world and compete with the skilled, trained minds, hands and eyes of men and women who have been trained in technical institutions. How can we do that unless we afford our people the proper facilities? How can the provinces provide the facilities under the conditions to which I have alluded? Nothing is more directly a branch of trade and commerce than technical education; therefore federal aid should be given.
Nor is there anything on which a greater dividend could be realized. I know of no other federal expenditure that could be made that would yield directly or indirectly a greater dividend to our people than money spent on technical education, and that is why the government should make the grant. We can appreciate this at once. Why discuss the necessity of technical education? Men do not discuss the necessity of pure air in which to breathe and live. Why should we discuss any longer the necessity of technical education? Without it the nation can have no permanent export trade, and because that is so, it is a branch of trade and commerce in the largest and best sense. It is true that its effects may be incorporated with those of industrial and scientific research, but the latter is the work of the laboratory, of the academic and trained mind. That is the work, as the doctor yonder will say, of the men who have had the special training which enables them to carry on scientific research in order to make discoveries that may in turn be utilized to the full by technically trained workers. Great inventions, important scientific discoveries, are being worked out in laboratories by men and women who are devoting their lives to that work; when their purposes are achieved, the industrialists, trained in mind, hand and eye, utilize those discoveries and inventions, and the resulting product is sold in the markets of the world by the Canadian people.
Let me summarize in these words my reasons for supporting the resolution: First, having created a condition by federal aid, we

Technical Education-Mr. Brady
must maintain it by federal aid until such aid is no longer required. Second, technical education is essentially a branch of trade and commerce, and therefore a federal matter, if this country's markets are to be extended and we are to compete successfully against the skilled and trained technicians that come from the great institutions of the old country and are now engaged in industrial work, sending their products to every part of the world. Lastly, technical education does not conflict with but is the complement of scientific research, by the aid of which, technical education will be made more effective. I trust that the administration will approach it from this point of view and agree without further consideration that it is desirable to renew for the next ten years, the aid that has been given in the past, so that we may take our place in exporting our products to the nations of the world.

Mr. Speaker, in support of the resolution of the member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich), may I say that technical education is a national duty relating to the economic development of Canada. I wish to repeat that for the benefit of those who are interested in this particular resolution; technical education is a national duty relating to the economic development of Canada. It seems to me a remarkable thing that this resolution should come from one who perhaps is not a Canadian by birth, because it deals in a very direct manner with our great immigration policy. I was more than disappointed when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) not this session but last, with that eloquence which he possesses, that gift of debate, that subtle ingenuity which characterize only a man of high accomplishment, attempted to prove that technical education was not part of the duty of the federal government.
The history of technical education in the modern world is a very interesting one. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) spoke of Germany and the part that technical education has played in furthering the wonderful industrial progress of that nation. England likewise has paid great attention to the development of technical education. Every nation places much importance upon technical education. What has been the result? We must judge the present in the light of the past, and I appeal to-night to the Prime Minister to trace the history of technical education in Canada. It is a very interesting story. Commercial courses were first introduced in Canada in the province Of Ontario, in 1899. They were introduced later in British Columbia in 1905 and to-night I wish to do honour to the old province of Quebec which was the first province to provide commercial courses for those pupils who did not desire to enter a university. The province of Quebec realized that thousands of their young people were not destined for university courses. They realized that only a limited number of the ten million people of Canada can hope for a university training and that the great pioneers of all progress in every department of trade, commerce, and industry have come from the rank and file of the common folk. They saw that there must be some opportunity provided for these young people to develop their talents and ability. Agricultural courses were first given in Ontario at the agricultural college at Guelph, in 1874, in Nova Scotia, in 1888; in the Manitoba college, in 1903; at the Macdonald college, in 1907. Training in handicrafts was introduced first in the schools in the form of manual training for the boys and domestic science for the girls. I wish for a moment to dwell upon the importance of technical training in these two departments.
Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, the wonderful effect produced in our educational work by manual training for the boys and domestic science for the girls? There is no part today of our educational system that is so fruitful, so beneficial in its results, as these two departments which to-day are menaced by the apathy, the indifference and lack of vision of the federal government, I marvel that a great party, representing as it does a very strong political view in Canada, can be so hopelessly inept, so indifferent to public opinion that it fails to realize that the one great thing needed for the building up of this young Dominion in its competition with older countries that have attained a considerable industrial development is the development of technical education in this country, and yet they prove themselves not merely incapable but hopelessly oblivious to the call which the interests of the country demand. '
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the Prime Minister; for him I have the deepest respect. I do believe that Canada has good men. I do believe that we are all taking a big part in the theatre of life in which we are called upon to act, whether we are stage boys or the hero in the play. But the Prime Minister to-night seemed to forget or desired to forget, that the federal government in times past placed itself behind the resolution of

Technical Education-Mr. Brady
the hon. member for Vegreville. Here is what I find:
Educational administration is assumed to be the concern of each province, nevertheless the Dominion government, recognizing the importance of technical education supplemented the provincial grants for these very purposes.
The Dominion government, the very government that ws are appealing to, has recognized that technical education was a national undertaking. I find that in 1913 the Agricultural Instruction Act was passed giving $10,000,000 over a period of ten years to the various provinces for the advancement of agricultural education. Furthermore, in 1919 a similar sum was voted to the provinces for technical education over a similar period of years.
What is the natural result of this? I submit that' it is undebatable, it is uneontradictable by any member on the government benches. The very grants given by the Dominion government have been most effective in turning the attention of the various provinces towards vocational education. But let us picture the various provinces to-day from the Pacific to the Atlantic, and what do we find? Owing to the support granted in past years by the Dominion government to technical education, the provinces entered upon the development of their technical schools, which they have developed to a stage that is today an honour to a young country like Canada. But let me direct the attention of the house to the disastrous results following the cessation of this federal aid. I rose to-night to tell the Prime Minister that the discontinuance of the federal aid for technical education had had' a most detrimental effect upon every technical school throughout British Columbia. When I was in Prince Rupert the other day I saw a letter from the provincial Minister of Education to the local school board regretting that the provincial government's contribution towards the upkeep of the domestic science department and the manual school had to be reduced.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this means that at a time when we are trying to build up industries in Canada-and we are next door to the greatest commercial and manufacturing country in the world-we are held down with, as it were, our hands tied behind our backs, denied the privilege of educating our boys and girls to take a part in the development of their native country. Is it fair, Mr. Speaker? No sir,
I tell the Prime Minister and I tell the government of Canada that there is nothing either human or divine that oan stop the feeling that surges in the breasts of the people of Canada because of this fact, that we are 
denied the right to assist every boy and girl, every young man and young woman, to participate in the gifts which a benign Providence has granted to us. I have sat in this house for four years, and at times I have suffered agony white I waited to know whether or not my view was wrong and that of other members was right. Last evening I heard the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) ridicule a very important resolution in that witty, felicitous manner that he possesses. After he finished I left the chamber and I said to myself: No, there is something yet to be done; somebody will rise some day in the house and tell us that hon. members do not always speak as they should in duty do. I do not in the least exaggerate when I say that we, the members of this honourable house, are honoured as few men can be honoured; money cannot buy the position that each of us holds in this house; it is the tribute of the people-
Oh, oh.

Oh, is that so? I think
otherwise. The people of Skeena put me here, and in return they expect at least that on a vital question pertaining to the welfare of Canada I should speak the truth. With the deepest sincerity I declare my belief that the government is acting very foolishly in not supporting the claims of the provinces for federal assistance towards the improvement of technical education, and, I heartily endorse the resolution of the hon. member for Vegreville. The people of Canada to-day are asking for the one thing which I am feebly trying to present, that is, that technical educational grants by the federal government are essential for the welfare of Canada. If we do not grant them we are traitors to Canada, to its young men and women who look to us to give them opportunities to live in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to detain the house at so late an hour, even momentarily, and certainly I would not do so were I not fully seized of the importance of the subject dealt with in the resolution now before the house. Indeed, if I allowed this occasion to go by without proferring some remarks I would feel that I was remiss in my duty to countless thousands of Canadian citizens who have not, on account of circumstances, been given the opportunity to receive an education in cur universities and in our schools of higher study.
I was very much interested, Mr. Speaker, in the excellent address of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). As I have listened to many of his addresses in this house I have come to the conclusion that

Technical Education-Mr. Macdougall
he always attains his highest degree of excellence when he defends the lack of responsibility of the government towards important issues concerning the welfare of the people of the different provinces of Canada. It would be well for us, if only in the interests of logic and of sound reasoning, to place in juxtaposition two of the statements of the right hon. gentleman to-night. He told us of his great belief in technical education. He made an open confession-which is supposed to be good for the soul but which is generally hard on the reputation-that he believed in technical education and was a great supporter of it; and in the very same breath he told us that there was no constitutional obstacle in the way of the federal government assisting the provinces in carrying on the work of technical education. What happens to his belief? The federal government has abounding revenues. The Prime Minister claims to believe in technical education, and has the desire to see it carried on in every province in Canada, and yet, with skilled evasion, he escapes the responsibility with respect to that in which he professes to be such a great believer.
He told us that one of the reasons why they were opposed to the resolution was that the prairie provinces were being given their natural resources and their subsidies. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, that is an unfair argument. Does the right hon. gentleman want to convey to this house the belief or the idea that the prairie provinces were not entitled to the return of their natural resources and to the financial arrangement that went along with them? That is a question that should not be mixed up with technical education at all. Coming as I do from the east, I believe that the prairie provinces are entitled to a greater measure of justice from the federal parliament than they have even now received, or rather are about to receive, in the case of one or two of them. And, so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, increased subsidies have been awarded to those provinces as the result of the recommendation of a commission appointed some four years ago. May I point out in this connection that the recommendations of that commission in respect to increased subsidies have not yet been carried out by the Prime Minister and his government? All that Sir Andrew Rae Duncan recommended was that there should be substantial increases in the subsidies to those provinces, and that pending such readjustment of subsidies interim lump sums should be paid immediately. Those interim lump sums to the maritime provinces were,
in the words of the Duncan commission, to represent the minimum of justice to which those provinces were entitled.
This question of technical education is one of imiportantee not only to the provinces but to the whole Dominion. My right hon. friend says that the provinces should carry it on, that they have the revenues with which to carry it on, and in support of that statement he proclaims, with great gusto, that no technical school has been closed because of the discontinuance of this grant for technical education. Of course no technical school has been closed in any of the provinces. Why? Because the provinces were alive to the need of technical education which my right hon. friend and his associates seem so fully to believe in; with their limited sources of revenue the provinces have carried on splendidly. But it is unfair to ask the provinces to carry on wholly a work which is of interest and of importance and value to the whole Dominion of Canada. My right hon. friend talks glibly about revenues and sources of revenue. There is only one source whence the federal government or any provincial government can obtain revenue ; that source is the Canadian people. My right hon. friend, by shirking his responsibility in this matter, creates a condition whereby the earning power of the people of this country is decreased, because knowledge is power; and if our people through technical education are enabled to seize the opportunities afforded by the economic advantages of this country, then our sources of revenue, 'both provincial and federal, will be increased.
Not only is it important for us to safeguard the revenues that we have, but we must safeguard above all else that source from which revenues are derived, the people of Canada. There is nothing but skilled evasion in the attitude taken by my right hon. friend tonight. There is no constitutional objection to giving grants for this purpose to the provinces. He says he believes in technical education. I say to him to-night, as a fellow-Canadian who wants to see every possible advantage in the matter of education placed within the reach of the common people of this country, let us make the grants, and the returns in the years to come will redound not only to the prosperity of the various provinces but to the advancement of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, just a few remarks on this subject. It appears that the house is unanimously in favour of technical education. The difference, as I see it, is that those who have spoken

Technical Education-Mr. Geary
on this side of the house desire to help along the cause of technical education, and, if I may say so, the arguments that have been adduced from the other side of the house all tend to hinder it.
I wish to refer more particularly to the argument of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). As far as I could gather, while he did not raise a constitutional abjection to the sipending of money on technical education, he did, in a roundabout way, invoke the old cry of unconstitutionality by seeking to delimit the powers or the obligations of the Dominion and the provinces in that regard. I could not quite follow the argument of the right hon. gentleman in regard to the expenditure of money by Great Britain. Surely he must see that there is no possible analogy between hypothetical help by Great Britain to the Dominion and help by the Dominion of Canada to the several provinces forming the confederation. There is no common taxation in the British Empire, and if our constitutional status, which for one reason or another has been urged so strongly, particularly on the other side of this house amounts to anything, it means that we are quite independent of each other in fiscal matters. I cannot follow my right hon. friend at all if he seeks to adduce that as an argument against the Dominion of Canada spending federal money in aid of the provincial exercise of power in education, and with relation to the particular branch known as technical education.
I am not very sure that we can refer advantageously to the British North America Act. All it says about education is that the provinces alone have power to make laws in regard to education. At the time the act was passed technical education probably was not contemplated by those who formulated it.. It was not in their minds, and it was not considered that there would be such an expenditure of money as is required to conduct technical education. True, it is a branch of education, but not within the contemplation of the parties to the agreement at that time.
The Prime Minister has said that in the year 1910 the Dominion government thought some start should be made in technical education, and to that end a committee was appointed. There is no doubt that it was the findings of that committee that first started the different provinces on the road to technical education, and because, as the Prime Minister has said, there was not enough money in the provinces to get the movement started, it was thought well that parliament should provide the initial expenditure.
* [Mr. Geary.)
Ten years have gone by, and we have found the amount of the grant very useful, although some of the provinces have not as yet been able to take full advantage of it. It is still in its infancy, so to speak, and when we ask the Dominion parliament to continue the grant for another ten years we are simply asking it to keep on its feet an institution which this Dominion parliament helped establish throughout the different provinces. To be sure, we cannot detail to the provinces how that money is to be spent, but I have not heard of a province refusing any grant that this parliament chooses to make, earmarked as that grant may be. The fact, that they accepted it very cheerfully ten years ago is enough to authorize us to go in the belief that they will cheerfully accept it in the future.
The other ground the Prime Minister urges against the expenditure of the money is that of economy. He asks why we should spend the sum of SI,000,000 per year. If I may say so, the right hon. gentleman adduced a very unfair argument, and one that should not be accepted without some protest from this side of the house. I do not think his statement was so much in the cause of Dominion legislation or Dominion powers as it was in the cause of the present government. He said that he would rather give money towards soldier pensions than to this project, if a choice were to be made between the two. I do not think any member of this house should be made to think for one minute that the amount of money to be paid in pensions to soldiers is to be influenced in either way, up or down, by the fact that parliament chooses to make a grant for technical education. I protest strongly against the Prime Minister holding a club, as it were, over this side of the house and appealing to the country by saying in effect that one reason for opposing this particular grant is to assist the cause of the soldiers. Let me assure the right hon. gentleman that he will find no objection whatever on this side of the house to the expenditure of any amount we think should be spent on behalf of our ex-service men.
There is one other point I would like to mention, and that is in regard to the subsidies that have been paid to the provinces. Those subsidies were originally made in full of all demands, under the British North America Act, which might be made at any future time by a province. As I say, this is not a demand by the provinces; it is a free gift to all the people of the country, a gift to which the Prime Minister says there is no objection whatever constitutionally. This house may grant the money; it is not in any sense a

Technical Education-Mr. Dunning
demand which could be set off against the subsidies, for the subsidies were given in full of all demands which the provinces might make at any future time in regard to the allocations then made by the British North America Act, in which allotment of subjects technical education was probably not considered.
It seems to me that the Prime Minister's whole speech went as an excuse, in some measure, for not supporting this particular grant. He says in so many words that he is in favour of technical education, yet he seeks, by constitutional argument and pleas of economy, in some way or another to find a basis for refusing to promote it. I cannot think why he persists in that attitude. I am pure his followers think he is wrong, as do the members who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker.
I trust that on reconsideration of the matter he will see that this is a proper and just allowance to be made by the Dominion in furtherance of a system which the Dominion itself has introduced, which operates not so much to the benefit of a province as to the benefit of all the people of Canada.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): This is another of the resolutions calling upon the Dominion government to make a grant to the provinces, as a matter pf grace, which it is not constitutionally obligated to make as a matter of right. It is for that reason I oppose the principle, just as I always opposed the principle of grants of this kind when I occupied the position of premier in a provincial government. My reasons I stated- briefly the other evening. I do not believe that directly or indirectly the federal parliament should seek to infringe upon the autonomy of the provinces in respect to matters which, under the constitution, they and they alone control.
There are many ways in which the central parliament, with its widier taxing powers, pan coerce the provinces. One is by offering free grants to the provinces, provided that those provinces adopt certain policies over which they alone have control, under the ponstitution. The Dominion, by holding out these offers of free grants by grace, can coerce the provinces to adopt policies whether or not they, as provinces, desire to adopt them. The leader of the opposition to-night indicated that one of the reasons why this grant should be continued for a further period of ten years was that the provinces had come to depend upon it. That to my mind, Mr. Speaker, is a reason why we should not adopt the principle behind this resolution. The provinces are absolutely dependent upon the grace of parliament to make grants of this description. If it is desirable that we should pay further money to the provinces for any purpose, then I argue that the British North America Act should be amended with respect to the per capita grants which the provinces receive from this parliament as a matter of constitutional right, and larger grants should be given to them by that method rather than by the method of grants which are matters of grace, and which can be withdrawn or withheld at any time at the whim or by the desire of the majority of this parliament.
May I ask the hon. gentleman how he proposes to amend the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In exactly the same way it has been amended on at least three or four occasions in respect to the same matter of enlargement of the per capita subsidies, which would have to 'be brought about by a conference between the provinces and the Dominion. That is the proper way to approach this matter, rather than by getting into the position in which, as the leadeT of the opposition admits, we now find ourselves, that of having made a grant to the provinces by grace, and finding at the end of the ten years that the provinces have come to depend upon something to which they have no real claim constitutionally. So the result is that they are compelled to come here as suppliants for something to be given to them as a matter of grace. I took that attitude as a member of a provincial administration when sums of money were offered to us for various purposes. I believe it is important, unless we are to develop in Canada a centralized system of government, that the provinces should be dealt with, so far as monetary relations with this parliament are concerned, upon the basis of right rather than upon the basis of grace.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member has
made his speech; will he kindly resume his seat and allow me to make mine? Does the hon. member desire to ask me a question or to make a speech?
To ask a question. The minister says that he took objection to the grants when he was a member of the government of Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Did he take the
grants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. As I stated before, it is a method of coercion in advance of their

Technical Education-Mr. Dunning
being ready to adopt it. Saskatchewan was unable, for reasons which were best known to itself and which were known very well to the people of the province, to take advantage immediately of the grants and has been taking advantage of them only for the past two or three years. My hon. friend's own province did not take advantage of the grants before and is only now taking advantage of them. The fact is that while the grants were first made available in 1919 only the wealthier ptovinces were able immediately to take advantage of them, with the result that now, more than ten years after the enactment of the original legislation, at least four if not five of the provinces have been unable to take advantage of it. Last year the act was extended for five years in order that those provinces might take advantage of what was made available more than ten years ago.
My hon. friends are asking for an extension of another ten years. For what provinces? Not for those who have not yet taken advantage of the grant which is still available and will be until 1934: it must be for the provinces which have had already the maximum of assistance, the provinces which have had the most money. Why? Because they have the greatest population, and the grant was based upon population; because, having the greatest population they have the greatest sources of revenue locally; and because having the greatest sources of revenue locally they were better able to meet their obligation under the legislation, the obligation being that the province should spend an amount of money at least equal to the amount spent by the Dominion government. The provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and I think one other province have not yet been able to do so, but they have five years in which to take advantage of the money available under the existing legislation. Any proposal to extend this scheme only can mean that the provinces which are now behind in taking advantage of it will be still further behind, and the provinces which have had the maximum advantage of it hitherto will continue to receive money from the federal government to carry on work which, I submit, they are well able financially to carry on for themselves.
What is the position to-day? When the time for payment expired under the original act there was still $2,035,000 available for the province which had not yet been able to take advantage of their full allotment, in some cases not being able to take advantage of the act at all. With all the complaint we have been receiving from the opposite side of the house regarding assistance for technical educa-

tion, we have paid out of the treasury this year for assistance to technical education not less than $465,000, and this amount has gone to those provinces which are least able to help themselves in regard to this matter. It has been paid to those provinces which in order to take advantage of this act have had to wait until they were financially able to bear fifty per cent of the burden imposed by the act.
I shall make only one brief reference to the division of work which was tentatively agreed on between the Dominion and the provinces at the last interprovincial conference. There was a very full discussion of the technical education system and of that higher realm of national work which is linked to it and which was referred to by the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the work of national research. All the provinces agreed that it was desirable that we should have in Canada a national research institution fully equipped with the latest scientific apparatus and manned with the best possible scientific brains in order to evolve those processes and methods which might best be applied to technical education. That is really the basic work of the national research organization of this country, and in the estimates which are now before the house is a sum of not less than $500,000 for the carrying on of that work for the coming fiscal year. How is it expended? It is expended in research work not only here at Ottawa, in the laboratories which are temporarily in operation, but in the universities in the different provinces, in scholarships in research in order that those universities may provide men to convey technical education and technical training to those who, more and more as time passes, go to the technical schools. I submit, sir, that when this Dominion is spending $500,000 a year on scientific research, when it is providing for the erection of national laboratories in the capital city to enable that work to be carried on effectively, which expenditure will run to $3,000,000 before the work is fully completed and the laboratories completly equipped; when it is doing that, and when it is continuing for another five years the grants to what I might call, not the poorer provinces-I do not care for that expression-but those provinces which have not yet been able to take advantage of the technical education grants; when it is continuing those grants for another five years in order to enable them to get the same start in technical education as the older and wealthier provinces have secured, then this Dominion has discharged to the full any moral obligation it is under in that regard. I do not consider that there is any con-

Technical Education-Mr. Kaiser
stitutional obligation, as I draw a clear line between what we must do constitutionally and what we may do as a matter of grace.
It is ridiculous to charge those who are setting forth the Dominion's responsibilities with being opposed to technical education. One might as well say that I am opposed to hospitals because I would not advocate a Dominion grant to be paid to hospitals. One might as well argue that I am opposed to general education because I would oppose the federal authorities making a grant to the public schools all over the Dominion. After all, Mr. Speaker, we have in this country a federal system of government, and we have set out as well as we could, in the statute which governs our relationships with each other, the obligations both provincial and federal. It may be that there is an argument in favour of enlarging the free subsidies now being paid by the Dominion to the provinces; that is arguable at least, but I do stand firmly behind the principle that each province should have the free right to expend the money which it receives either from its own taxation or from the subsidies from the Dominion treasury. It should be subject in that regard to no coercion, legislative or otherwise, by the parliament of the Dominion of Canada.
Before the hon. minister takes his seat, I would ask him if he does not think that the principle of grants to technical education is identical with the grants in respect to old age pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree that they are the same at all.

Mr. Speaker, I will not either assume nor presume to follow the argument of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) but I rise merely to say that for once I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Finance minister (Mr. Dunning) upon one thing- absolute consistency for once.
I will illustrate what I mean. In the city from which I come there is on one side of the road a splendid industry, one which requires more technical hands than any other industry in the city-I do not mean the automobile business. These people have been asking for trained young men and young women to help them in their industry.
What is the industry?

Fittings Limited, makers of all kinds of fittings and castings. They are addressing themselves to the manufacture of some of the parts of automobiles that have
hitherto been made in the United States. These people asked for a technical school. Last year or the year before we spent $300,000 or $400,000 to build a technical school to turn out the youth of the land equipped to work in this particular industry. Owing to the drift of policy of the present government, a resolution came before the house a few days ago asking for a reduction in the tariff in regard to the goods that these people manufacture, and yesterday I received this telegram which I want to read:
Have just been instructed by Canadian supplier of transmissions for trucks to hold up orders for castings involving about 100 tons owing to possible revision of the duty to 6 per cent. This would be a serious blow to Canadian workmen and we respectfully urge vigorous opposition.
J. D. Storie.
That is the president of Fittings Limited. As I see this technical school arise, training our youth for work in this industry, and as I see this industry crumbling owing to the attitude, .policy and principles of the government, I say that the two things are absolutely inconsistent and we should vote exactly as they ask. Why should we spend our money in building technical schools when the government destroy the only industries in Canada that our boys can work in?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one can derive a good deal of amusement from the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite. Let me deal just for a moment or two with the statement of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) who has just addressed the house. He has accused the government of being guilty of bringing in a motion to reduce the tariff on automobiles.
I beg the minister's pardon. I did not say the government. I said that a resolution was before the house along the line of the general policy of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is imputing motives, I have no reply to make to that except to say that I am always in favour of reduction of duty, but that has nothing to do with the question before the house at the moment. As I understand the matter, my hon. friend is seriously supporting the motion of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) and he finds a great deal of fault with the motion to which he has just referred, moved by the hon. member for Macfeod (Mr. Coote). Therefore,, if he is to be consistent, he cannot support, those hon. gentlemen in both motions.
592	COMMONS
Technical Education-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
The motion before the house calls upon the government of Canada to give further consideration to technical education. I do not propose to make any lengthy statement with respect to technical education or its value to the Canadian people, but I wish to direct the attention particularly of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) and the hon. member for Ontario to the fact that there is a clear line of duty marked out for the federal government and the provincial authority. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has very properly said, the provinces have assumed continuously the responsibility for education, and I cannot conceive of any hon. member moving a resolution asking for federal aid to education. I was in identically the same position as the present Minister of Finance, in his capacity as a member of the provincial government, with respect to the grants by the federal government in aid of highway construction. There is no desire to avoid responsibility. I am a taxpayer in the province of Alberta, and I have no desire to avoid responsibility for taxation for carrying on technical education. As former premier of Alberta I am rather proud of the fact that we lent the aid, and furnished the money for the construction of the technical school which is now operating in Calgary and of which my hon. friend has spoken so glowingly to-night, and I am proud of the work it is doing for the youth of Alberta. But surely there is some place where the responsibility of the provinces ends and that of the federal government begins, and the responsibility in educational matters is not of federal concern. As I said the other day with respect to the motion dealing with grants towards highway construction, in all these matters it is the easiest thing in the world for an hon. member to rise in his place and call upon the federal government to make grants in respect to matters of provincial concern. Hon. gentlemen opposite have a habit of calling upon the federal government to provide, from taxes collected by it, grants to the provinces for matters that are purely of provincial concern.

The government boasted
so much of its surplus.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
May I point out that it was in my hon. friend's province that they boasted a great deal about the surplus shown in the budget recently presented to the legislature at Toronto? The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) waxed

eloquent to-night and called upon the people of Canada and high heaven to witness how recreant this government were in their duty, but only two days ago he was calling upon high heaven to witness how recreant we were because we were not building a road into Prince Rupert. High heaven witnesses a lot of recreancies of that character, and I have no doubt that if we were to meet his request he would come forward with some other resolution calling upon the government, because it happened to have a surplus, to make a grant to the provincial government for some other purpose.
May I say that so far as the duties of the federal and provincial authorities are concerned, if the provinces require more assistance, let them come forward and say so and I shall be glad to assist in having their subsidies increased. Let them do as they wish with the money grants.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
